accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England English programmes of study: Year 1 and Year 2 writing transcription (write from memory simple sentences dictated by the teacher that include words using the GPCs and common exception words taught so far; Year 2 adds punctuation taught so far) and English Appendix 1 (ck just after a short vowel, ay at the end of words and ai not at the end, igh and oa for long vowels, said/was/they/the/have/come/one on the Year 1 common exception list). Common Core L.1.2d, L.1.2e and L.2.2d were read from the standard text; every lab word was checked for its phoneme count and grapheme.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented dictation slips: dropping small words (step 1 prediction 'I can see a cat' as 4 words, wrong-count feedback naming a, is and at; mastery m3), counting letters as sounds (step 2 prediction ship as s-h-i-p, challenge chip; practice p1), choosing the wrong grapheme for a position (ay mid-word in rain, k after a short vowel in duck, i for igh in night), spelling exception words by sound (sed, woz, thay, cum, wun in step 3; challenge thay/thai), and forgetting the capital, I and full stop (step 5; challenge i can run / I can run without a stop).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdictate is built around writing from memory: tap the word count for a heard sentence, fill phoneme boxes one sound at a time from a meaning clue (no word shown), choose a whole-word exception spelling, read a sentence, hide it and rebuild it word by word from memory by dragging cards past a distractor, then proofread a written sentence for capital, full stop and exception-word slips. lab_distinct kept it under 30% against flagendread, flagdecode, flagtrick and every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each habit is met by doing it: tapping 7 for 'My mum got a big red hat' returns 'Count again. Did you count the little word a?'; picking s for /sh/ returns 'sh is one sound made by two letters. Both go in one box'; picking sed returns 'sed is how it sounds, but the real spelling is said. Look, cover, write, check'; after Hide it, the sentence must be rebuilt in order, so holding it in mind is the task itself. Done screens list the counts, the grapheme splits (duck: d | u | ck) and the corrected sentences.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions hold a tempting wrong answer that the step disproves: 4 words in 'I can see a cat' (skipping a), ship as four sounds s-h-i-p (the boxes show three), and that said can be spelt by its sounds s-e-d (the tricky-word step shows it cannot). The done line repeats the learner's prediction and the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve distinct wrong-answer messages: letters counted as sounds in chip, sounds merged, thay and thai as sound spellings of they, ay used mid-word, single a for /ai/, a skipped word and a double-counted word in 'We ran to the bus', lower-case i, a missing full stop, k after a short vowel and c alone in sock. The lab steps add a specific message for every wrong count, grapheme, spelling, word order and proofreading tap.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (Count the words on your fingers. Now you can hold it in your head.) and pass the family readability limit in validate_lessons. The canvas uses 24–32 px words on white or cream cards, one instruction per round, and long feedback wraps onto two lines after the first screenshots showed it squeezed. The adult text uses the precise terms GPC, phoneme, grapheme, digraph, trigraph, segmenting and common exception word.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no banned phrases and the explanation stayed under the 12% six-word overlap limit against every lesson, including Reading Inflectional Endings, Tricky words, Decoding unfamiliar words and Using a Dictionary to Check Spellings. Every feedback line names the word, the sound or the rule that matters.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, light and dark) for all six steps at the start, after a wrong tap and after Show me: four number tiles fit one row, three phoneme boxes and two 68 px grapheme cards fit, the hide-and-rebuild step keeps the answer shelf above two rows of word cards, and the proofreading chips wrap with a 56 px minimum width so a one-letter word like I is still a big target. The rebuild cards were moved up after the first screenshot showed feedback overlapping the second row.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge showed, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark. Every canvas action has a labelled large button ('5 words', 'Spell the sound with sh', 'The spelling is said', 'Hide the sentence', 'Next word: cat', 'sed has a slip'), the young class gives 56 px buttons, and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with every feedback line. No step needs sound: the clue text or a grown-up does the dictating.
